topics.title: Loading Scripts: defer, async & type="module"
topics.summary: Control when JavaScript downloads and runs so it never blocks HTML parsing.
topics.description:
By default a `<script src>` is **parser-blocking**: the browser stops building the page, downloads the file, runs it, then continues. That delays rendering. Two attributes fix this.

### The three modes
| Attribute | Download | Executes | Order | DOM ready? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | blocks parser | immediately | in order | No |
| `defer` | parallel | after HTML parsed, before DOMContentLoaded | **in order** | Yes |
| `async` | parallel | as soon as downloaded | **unpredictable** | Maybe |
| `type="module"` | parallel | deferred by default | module graph | Yes |

### Choosing
- **App code that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts** → `defer` (put the tag in `<head>`).
- **Independent scripts** such as analytics or ads → `async`.
- **Modern ES modules** (`import`/`export`) → `type="module"`; it is deferred automatically, strict mode, own scope.
- Old habit: scripts at the end of body. `defer` in head is better because the download starts early.

### More
- `nomodule` - run only in browsers that do not support modules.
- `<script type="importmap">` - bare specifier mapping.
- `<noscript>` - fallback content.
- Inline scripts ignore `defer`/`async` (except modules, which are always deferred).
- Add `integrity` and `crossorigin` for CDN files (Subresource Integrity).

### CSS also blocks
Stylesheets in head block rendering (to avoid unstyled flashes) and block scripts below them. Keep CSS small and critical.
keyPoints: Plain script blocks HTML parsing.
defer: parallel download, runs after parsing, keeps order.
async: runs as soon as ready, order not guaranteed.
type="module" is deferred by default and has its own scope.
Use defer for app code, async for independent third parties.
pitfalls: Using async for scripts that depend on each other.
Using defer on inline scripts - it has no effect.
Placing blocking scripts in head with no defer.

examples.title: The three ways in the head
examples.code:
<head>
  <!-- blocks parsing: avoid -->
  <script src="legacy.js"></script>

  <!-- best for your app: runs after HTML is parsed, in order -->
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- independent: analytics, ads -->
  <script src="analytics.js" async></script>

  <!-- modern modules: deferred automatically -->
  <script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
</head>

examples.title: Execution order demo
examples.html: Order printed above shows module scripts waiting for parsing.
examples.explanation: Module scripts run after the document has been parsed, but before DOMContentLoaded.

interview.a: Both download in parallel. defer executes after parsing in document order; async executes as soon as downloaded in any order.
No. type="module" scripts are deferred by default.
In head with defer (or at the end of body for older practice) so they do not block rendering.

topics.title: Resource Hints: preload, prefetch, preconnect
topics.summary: Tell the browser early what it will need so it can fetch or connect ahead of time.
topics.description: Browsers discover resources while parsing. **Resource hints** in `` let you tell them about important resources earlier. | Hint | What it does | Use for | |---|---|---| | `rel="preload"` | Fetch a resource **now**, high priority, for *this* page | hero image, key font, critical CSS/JS | | `rel="prefetch"` | Fetch at **low priority** for a *future* navigation | next page's script/data | | `rel="preconnect"` | Open DNS + TCP + TLS to an origin early | CDN, API, fonts domain | | `rel="dns-prefetch"` | Only resolve DNS early | many third parties | | `rel="modulepreload"` | Preload an ES module and its dependencies | module apps | | `rel="prerender"` / Speculation Rules | Render the next page in the background | likely next click | ### Syntax ```html ``` ### Rules - `as` is **required** for preload so the browser sets priority and cache correctly. - Fonts need `crossorigin` even on the same origin. - Do not preload everything - too many hints compete with truly critical resources and waste bandwidth. - A preload that is not used within a few seconds triggers a console warning. ### fetchpriority `` raises the priority of the LCP image without a preload tag.
keyPoints: preload = needed now; prefetch = maybe needed next.
preconnect warms up the connection to another origin.
preload requires the as attribute (and crossorigin for fonts).
Over-preloading hurts performance.
fetchpriority="high" prioritises the key image.
pitfalls: Preloading without as.
Preloading resources that are never used.
Forgetting crossorigin on font preloads (fetched twice).

examples.title: Typical hints for a fast hero page
examples.code:
<head>
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
  <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/Inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
  <link rel="preload" href="/img/hero.avif" as="image" fetchpriority="high">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/main.css">
  <link rel="prefetch" href="/pricing.html">
</head>
examples.explanation: Dev tools Network panel shows the Priority column so you can verify the effect.

interview.a: preload fetches a resource needed for the current page at high priority; prefetch fetches something that may be needed for a future navigation at low priority.
It performs DNS lookup, TCP connection and TLS handshake to an origin ahead of the request, saving time.

topics.title: Lazy Loading Images & iframes
topics.summary: loading="lazy" delays offscreen images and iframes until the user scrolls near them.
topics.description: Loading every image on page load wastes bandwidth and slows the first view. **Lazy loading** defers images and iframes that are off-screen. ```html ``` ### Values - `loading="lazy"` - load when near the viewport. - `loading="eager"` - load immediately (default). ### Rules of thumb - **Do not** lazy-load the first visible (above-the-fold / LCP) image - it makes the page slower. Use `fetchpriority="high"` instead. - Always set `width` and `height` so lazy images do not cause layout shift. - Great for long articles, galleries, comment avatars and embedded videos/maps. - Images in ``: put `loading` on the inner ``. ### Other lazy techniques - **IntersectionObserver** for custom behaviour (videos, background images, infinite scroll). - `
keyPoints: loading="lazy" works on img and iframe.
Never lazy-load the LCP / above-the-fold image.
Set width and height to avoid layout shifts.
IntersectionObserver gives custom lazy loading.
Fully safe as progressive enhancement.
pitfalls: Lazy-loading the hero image and hurting LCP.
No dimensions on lazy images - the page jumps while scrolling.
Lazy-loading tiny icons - it adds overhead.

interview.q: How do you lazy load an image?
interview.a: Add loading="lazy" to the img (or iframe); the browser loads it only when it is near the viewport.

interview.q: Which images should NOT be lazy loaded?
interview.a: Above-the-fold images, especially the Largest Contentful Paint image.

topics.title: Web Storage: localStorage & sessionStorage
topics.summary: Store key-value strings in the browser: persistent with localStorage, per-tab with sessionStorage.
topics.description:
Web Storage is a simple key-value store in the browser (about 5 MB per origin). It replaced many uses of cookies.

| | localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Until cleared | Until tab closes | Set by expiry |
| Scope | Origin (all tabs) | Origin + single tab | Origin (+ path) |
| Sent to server | No | No | Yes, with every request |
| Size | ~5 MB | ~5 MB | ~4 KB |

### API
```js
localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
localStorage.getItem('theme');      // 'dark' (null if missing)
localStorage.removeItem('theme');
localStorage.clear();
localStorage.length; localStorage.key(0);
```

### Only strings
Convert objects with JSON:
```js
localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify({ name: 'Asha' }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user'));
```

### The storage event
When another tab changes localStorage, a `storage` event fires in the other tabs - a simple way to sync tabs.

### Security & limits
- Synchronous (blocks the main thread) - keep data small.
- Readable by any script on the page, so **never store passwords or tokens** that XSS could steal (prefer HttpOnly cookies).
- Can throw in private mode or when full - wrap in try/catch.
- Use IndexedDB for large or structured data.
keyPoints: localStorage persists; sessionStorage lasts for the tab.
Only strings - use JSON.stringify/parse for objects.
About 5 MB per origin; synchronous API.
Not sent to the server automatically (unlike cookies).
Never store secrets in web storage.
pitfalls: Storing objects without JSON.stringify - you get "[object Object]".
Treating localStorage as secure.
Not handling exceptions when storage is blocked or full.

examples.title: Persist a counter and a theme
examples.html: Visits stored: 0
examples.explanation: Always try/catch storage access: it may be unavailable in sandboxed frames or private mode.

interview.a: localStorage persists indefinitely per origin, sessionStorage lasts for the tab session, and cookies are small, can expire and are sent with every HTTP request.

interview.q: How do you store an object in localStorage?
interview.a: Serialize with JSON.stringify when saving and JSON.parse when reading.
Not really; any XSS can read it. HttpOnly cookies are safer for session tokens.

topics.title: Geolocation API
topics.summary: Ask the user for permission and read latitude/longitude with navigator.geolocation.
topics.description:
The **Geolocation API** lets a page learn the user's position (with explicit permission). It works only in **secure contexts** (HTTPS or localhost).

### Getting the position once
```js
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
  (pos) => {
    const { latitude, longitude, accuracy } = pos.coords;
  },
  (err) => console.log(err.code, err.message),
  { enableHighAccuracy: true, timeout: 8000, maximumAge: 0 }
);
```

### Watching movement
`navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(success, error, options)` returns an id; stop with `clearWatch(id)`.

### Error codes
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 | PERMISSION_DENIED |
| 2 | POSITION_UNAVAILABLE |
| 3 | TIMEOUT |

### Options
- `enableHighAccuracy` - GPS (slower, more battery).
- `timeout` - ms to wait.
- `maximumAge` - accept a cached position this old.

### Good practice
- Ask only after a user action ("Find stores near me"), never on page load.
- Explain *why* you need it.
- Always handle denial and provide manual fallback (type your city).
- Location is sensitive personal data - do not store it without need.

### Permissions Policy
In an iframe the parent must allow it: `<iframe allow="geolocation">`.
keyPoints: navigator.geolocation requires user permission and HTTPS.
getCurrentPosition = once; watchPosition = continuous.
Always implement the error callback (denied/timeout).
Request location only after a user gesture.
iframes need allow="geolocation".
pitfalls: Requesting location on page load.
No fallback when permission is denied.
Forgetting accuracy - coordinates may be rough (IP based).

topics.title: Drag and Drop API
topics.summary: Make elements draggable and handle dragstart, dragover and drop events.
topics.description:
The HTML Drag and Drop API makes native dragging of elements and files possible.

### Steps
1. Mark the source: `draggable="true"` (images, links and selected text are draggable by default).
2. Listen for **`dragstart`** on the source - store data with `event.dataTransfer.setData('text/plain', id)`.
3. On the target, handle **`dragover`** and call `event.preventDefault()` - this is what *allows* dropping.
4. Handle **`drop`** - call `preventDefault()`, read `getData()` and move/append the element.

### Events
| Event | Fires on | When |
|---|---|---|
| `dragstart` | source | drag begins |
| `drag` | source | repeatedly while dragging |
| `dragenter` / `dragleave` | target | pointer enters/leaves |
| `dragover` | target | continuously over the target |
| `drop` | target | released |
| `dragend` | source | finished |

### File drop
Dropping files from the desktop: read `event.dataTransfer.files` in the `drop` handler (and prevent the default so the browser does not open the file).

### dataTransfer
- `effectAllowed` / `dropEffect` - copy, move, link.
- `setDragImage()` - custom ghost image.

### Accessibility
Native drag and drop is mouse centred. Provide a **keyboard alternative** (buttons "move up/down", select + move).

For complex sortable lists many projects use libraries, but the native API is enough for simple cases.
keyPoints: draggable="true" + dragstart start a drag.
dragover must call preventDefault to allow dropping.
Read data in drop via dataTransfer.getData.
Files can be dropped via dataTransfer.files.
Provide a keyboard alternative.
pitfalls: Forgetting preventDefault in dragover - drop never fires.
Not preventing default on drop - the browser navigates to the file.
No keyboard alternative for the same action.

topics.title: Web Workers (Background Threads)
topics.summary: Run heavy JavaScript in a separate thread so the UI never freezes.
keyPoints: Workers run JS in a background thread.
No DOM access; communicate with postMessage/onmessage.
Data is copied (structured clone) unless transferred.
terminate() stops a worker; close() inside stops itself.
Service workers enable offline PWAs.
pitfalls: Trying to touch document inside a worker.
Sending huge objects back and forth repeatedly (copy cost).
Starting a worker for trivial tasks.

examples.title: Heavy loop in a worker, UI stays responsive
examples.html:
Counter while working: 0

Click the button.
examples.explanation: The counter keeps ticking because the loop runs in the worker, not the main thread.

interview.a: A script running in a background thread, separate from the main UI thread, communicating by messages.

interview.q: Can a worker access the DOM?
interview.a: No. It has no access to document or window; it must post messages to the main thread.
A web worker offloads computation for a page; a service worker is a persistent proxy between page and network used for offline caching, push notifications and PWAs.
